items.summary: It is generally safe for older adults without a history of cardiovascular disease to discontinue statins for primary prevention, according to a study published online Nov. 7 in the New England Journal of Medicine to coincide with the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held from Nov. 6 to 9 in Chicago.

items.title: STAT+: Enforcement of stringent Medicaid work requirements delayed for six months
items.summary:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration announced Friday that it is giving states an additional six months to begin enforcing Medicaid work requirements.

States have been racing to prepare their Medicaid systems by Jan. 1 to include the work requirements passed last year in the One Big Beautiful Bill. The legislation required states that expanded Medicaid after Democrats passed the Affordable Care Act to ensure all working-age recipients without dependent children are employed, in school, or volunteering at least 80 hours each month, unless they are disabled, caring for young children, or “medically frail.” 

A federal judge recently rejected the federal government’s medical frailty definition and ruled that states did not have adequate time or resources to overhaul their eligibility systems.

Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…
items.t: STAT+: Enforcement of stringent Medicaid work requirements delayed for six months

items.title: STAT+: Democrats coalesce around ‘Medicare for More,’ ‘Medikids’ proposals
items.summary:
WASHINGTON — Democrats are coalescing around a plan to offer Medicare to more Americans, if not all of them.

As the party navigates the pressure to quickly lower the cost of living, so-called Medicare for More is emerging as a consensus policy that could avert divisions between the party’s moderate and liberal wings. 

A “ Medikids” proposal to provide free health insurance to everyone from birth until age 26 also is gaining traction among Democrats. 

Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…
items.t: STAT+: Democrats coalesce around ‘Medicare for More,’ ‘Medikids’ proposals

items.title: Can a scent really sharpen your memory? It's complicated
items.summary: The sense of smell shares an intimate but mysterious connection with memory. We know that past experiences can flash vividly to mind if we smell a scent that accompanied them. This has led to claims that aromatherapy can enhance memory or even diminish cognitive decline. But the mechanisms by which the brain associates experience with scent are still being unraveled, and there is mixed scientific evidence to back up such claims.
items.t: Can a scent really sharpen your memory? It's complicated

items.title: Air pollution exposure tied to atopic dermatitis in children
items.summary: Air pollution exposure is associated with increased atopic dermatitis (AD) prevalence in children, according to a review published online Nov. 9 in JAMA Pediatrics.
items.t: Air pollution exposure tied to atopic dermatitis in children

items.title: RNA switch lets drugs control gene therapy protein production
items.summary: Bioengineers at the University of California San Diego have developed a technology that allows drugs to control when cells produce therapeutic proteins, which could potentially make gene therapies safer and more adaptable for treating chronic diseases.
items.t: RNA switch lets drugs control gene therapy protein production

items.title: Personalized therapies for Crohn's and ulcerative colitis may follow from method that identifies harmful gut bacteria
items.summary: Which gut bacteria contribute to the development or worsening of chronic inflammation? An international research team led by Dr. Lukas Mager from University Hospital Tübingen and Prof. Kathy McCoy from the University of Calgary has developed an approach to identify and selectively target such bacteria. The researchers identified two bacterial species that promote intestinal inflammation and compounds that selectively inhibit their growth. Published in the journal Gut, the study could pave the way for personalized therapies for inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
items.t: Personalized therapies for Crohn's and ulcerative colitis may follow from method that identifies harmful gut bacteria

items.title: GLP-1s often contain untested additive combinations, study finds
items.summary: Use of GLP-1 receptor agonist medications (GLP-1s) has skyrocketed in recent years, and many people are using "compounded" GLP-1 products: medicines that include GLP-1s as well as other active substances, some of which are not regulated by the FDA. A new study found that compounded GLP-1s now make up a large majority of weight-loss medicines, commonly containing vitamin B12 analogs that have not been tested for safety in combination with GLP-1s.
items.t: GLP-1s often contain untested additive combinations, study finds

items.title: New addiction society guidance on medetomidine’s brutal withdrawal
items.t: New addiction society guidance on medetomidine’s brutal withdrawal

items.title: New body map traces origins of complex movements in the brains of mice
items.summary: A new biological blueprint of how the body of a mouse is represented in its brain could help scientists answer a fundamental question: How do we perform complex motions that use more than one body part, such as coordinating arm, hand, head and lips to sip a spoonful of soup? The study was published in Nature Communications.
items.t: New body map traces origins of complex movements in the brains of mice

items.title: A microbe-made molecule may reverse gut damage by boosting NAD levels
items.summary: Scientists at Rutgers Health have discovered a molecule produced by "good" gut bacteria that rapidly heals the intestinal lining, protecting against severe inflammatory diseases and triggering increased production of a coenzyme whose levels diminish with age.
items.t: A microbe-made molecule may reverse gut damage by boosting NAD levels

items.title: Longer inhibitory connections can push simulated neural networks beyond critical tipping point
items.summary: In neuroscience, the brain criticality hypothesis proposes that neurons in the brain are arranged in such a way that neural activity lies at or near a transition point between two extremes: an ordered state where neural activity dies out quickly and a disordered state where neural activity tends to spread quickly and potentially grow uncontrollably. This transition point is known as criticality, while the two activity regimes on either side of it are known as subcritical and supercritical, respectively.
items.t: Longer inhibitory connections can push simulated neural networks beyond critical tipping point

items.title: Forever chemical disturbs early development in stem cell model
items.summary: Research using stem cell-derived models of early human development suggests that PFOS, a persistent substance belonging to the PFAS group, can interfere with processes critical for early germ cell and embryonic development. items.title: Blood NAD levels track heart disease, not aging, study of more than 1,000 adults finds

items.title: Petroleum-based lubricants linked to MS risk
items.summary: A new study from Karolinska Institutet has shown that people with multiple sclerosis (MS) were more likely than people without the disease to report that they had been exposed to petroleum-based lubricants at work. The work is published in the journal Neurology.
items.t: Petroleum-based lubricants linked to MS risk

items.title: Mapping an enzyme offers clues to treating rare genetic disease
items.summary: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have mapped an enzyme that could be targeted to develop new treatments for glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1), a rare genetic disorder that can lead to brain damage, revealing new details about how the enzyme works and how its activity is controlled. The findings were published in Science Advances.
items.t: Mapping an enzyme offers clues to treating rare genetic disease

items.title: Some ketogenic diets found to cause mitochondrial stress and lead to inflammation

items.t: Some ketogenic diets found to cause mitochondrial stress and lead to inflammation

items.title: Early changes linked to ovarian cancer may leave a trace in the blood—new study
items.summary: The most common type of ovarian cancer tends to grow quickly. It's called high-grade serous ovarian cancer and often starts in a fallopian tube, one of the tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries toward the uterus.
items.t: Early changes linked to ovarian cancer may leave a trace in the blood—new study

items.title: Giving AI a 'childhood' offers insights into language development
items.summary: Every parent has watched it happen, and no scientist can fully explain how. A baby enters the world unable to understand a single word. Within a few years, that child recognizes thousands of words, follows complex sentences and communicates their own thoughts.

items.title: Final trial results show promising long-term survival with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab in advanced thymic tumors

items.t: Final trial results show promising long-term survival with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab in advanced thymic tumors

items.title: Drug safety information must remain accessible as patients move from websites to AI
items.summary: A prescription drug warning can be accurate and still be difficult for a patient to use. What matters is not only the information itself but also how and where people receive it. This becomes especially important as patients increasingly use AI systems to find answers about medications, sometimes without visiting the original source.
items.t: Drug safety information must remain accessible as patients move from websites to AI

items.title: Congenital syphilis rates soared in US newborns from 2012 to 2022
items.summary: Congenital syphilis rates among U.S. newborns increased nearly sixfold from 2012 to 2022, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The data show rising rates across all demographics and income levels, with the sharpest increases among Native Americans.
items.t: Congenital syphilis rates soared in US newborns from 2012 to 2022

items.title: Blocking excess scarring helps prevent heart failure development
items.summary: Most heart failure cases are caused to a large degree by a buildup of excess scar tissue in the heart, which currently has no treatments. Now, researchers have successfully prevented the development of severe heart failure in a mouse model of heart attack by blocking a protein that triggers the formation of excessive scar tissue.
items.t: Blocking excess scarring helps prevent heart failure development

items.title: STAT+: Senators introduce bill to curb conflicts of interest on preventive care panel
items.summary:
WASHINGTON — Two senators are introducing a bill Friday to rein in conflicts of interest on an influential federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services.

The bill, from Sens. Angus King (I-Maine) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), follows reports that a number of members picked by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. could profit from the decisions they make on the panel, known as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. It would codify standards for membership on the panel and for avoiding conflicts of interest.

The bill comes after STAT reported that members of the panel hold stock in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and that two of them own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care. The New York Times reported on the financial investments as well. Federal officials granted all members blanket waivers, allowing them to remain on the panel, though they could still be required to recuse themselves from particular matters. The panel has not met in more than a year. 

Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…
items.t: STAT+: Senators introduce bill to curb conflicts of interest on preventive care panel

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
items.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.

items.title: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy
items.summary: A study of more than 750,000 pregnancies found that early exposure to Ozempic, Wegovy, and similar drugs was not linked to increased pregnancy complications when used for weight loss, but was associated with a higher risk of premature birth when prescribed for diabetes. The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.

items.summary:
This is the second of two pieces about the experiencing of pre-clinical Alzheimer’s. Read the first here . 

In 1976, at the dawn of the modern Alzheimer’s era, the neurologist Robert Katzman, champion of efforts to extract Alzheimer’s from senility and “normal aging,” concluded his short essay “ The prevalence and malignancy of Alzheimer disease ” with this notably qualified call to action:

“In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.”

items.title: STAT+: Scientists debut map of basal ganglia, a key brain region involved in an array of diseases
items.summary:
A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.

Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer.

items.title: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
items.summary: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.

items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

items.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
items.summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.
items.t: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

items.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.
items.t: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

items.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.
items.t: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

items.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
items.summary: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.
items.t: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

items.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
items.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.
items.t: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

items.title: Senior doctors call off two-day strike planned this month
items.summary: Consultants in England were due to walk out on 25 November in disputes over pay and working conditions.
items.t: Senior doctors call off two-day strike planned this month

items.title: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts
items.summary: Ancient manuscripts, including the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, have revealed traces of a deadly sheep virus whose history stretches back more than 3,700 years. Scientists discovered that the virus has remained remarkably unchanged for millennia, turning historic parchment into an unexpected record of ancient disease outbreaks.
items.t: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

items.title: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
items.summary:
Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.

(Image credit: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi)
items.t: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak

items.title: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review
items.summary: Baroness Casey criticises variability of services and fees charged to self-funders in England.
items.t: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review

items.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
items.summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.
items.t: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

items.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
items.summary: New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.
items.t: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

items.title: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds
items.summary: Three pills came top and outperformed Prozac for preventing relapse in a large number of patients.
items.t: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds

items.title: Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
items.summary:
Renewed fighting has pushed Ethiopia's healthcare system close to collapse: "The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," one surgeon says of a brutal week in September.

(Image credit: AFP)
items.t: Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling

items.title: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds
items.summary: A major review of more than 350 studies suggests that eating less protein could slow aging, improve metabolic health, and potentially extend lifespan, challenging the widespread belief that more protein is always better. Researchers warn that many sedentary adults may be consuming too much protein, while emphasizing that individual needs depend on age and physical activity.
items.t: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

items.title: Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
items.summary:
School Girls; Or the African Mean Girls Play during opening night curtain call for the play's Broadway run this fall. In this final week of performances, livestreaming is available. Left to right: Jordan Rice, Nia Otchere-Sarfo, Lucia Aremu, Denee Benton, Heather Alicia Simms, Erin Morton, Jasmine Amy Rogers and Patina Miller.'/> "School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play," is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts. We interviewed the Tony-nominated playwright, Jocelyn Bioh.

(Image credit: Bruce Glikas)
items.t: Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you

items.title: Why honesty is not always the best policy
items.summary:
Should you tell your boss she's got food on her face? Your partner you hate their outfit? Social psychologist Vanessa Bohns shares advice on when to tell someone the truth — or keep your mouth shut.

(Image credit: Abi Inman/NPR)
items.t: Why honesty is not always the best policy

items.title: How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles
items.summary:
In Pennsylvania, health officials use a quiet vaccination campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been hit hard by the measles outbreak.

(Image credit: Daniel Vasta for NPR)
items.t: How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles

items.title: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low
items.summary: Even when bad cholesterol is brought down to healthy levels, some people remain at risk of heart attacks, and scientists may have discovered why. Researchers identified two types of fat-carrying particles that appear to promote inflammation and damage blood vessels through mechanisms beyond cholesterol buildup.
items.t: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

items.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
items.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.
items.t: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

items.title: How Medicaid affected one California House race
items.summary: A Republican in California's Central Valley fended off challengers for years. But his district had a lot of people on Medicaid, and he lost by a large margin this time.
items.t: How Medicaid affected one California House race

items.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.
items.t: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
items.summary: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.
items.t: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

items.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
items.summary: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.
items.t: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

items.title: A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a buildup of a protein called Miro1 may be a hidden driver of insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes, with preclinical experiments showing that removing it restores the muscles’ response to insulin. Exercise was also found to lower Miro1 levels in people with diabetes, revealing a potential new pathway for treating the disease.
items.t: A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

items.title: What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?
items.summary: The theory of ‘Love Languages’ has no scientific origin but it's often still mentioned in modern dating.
items.t: What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?
